SystemSketch · Block, Ports & Edges · 1 Sep 2026

The boundary
has no inside.

Your cable is refused because a SystemSketch port has exactly one direction, and an Expanded block's boundary needs two: from outside, raw bytes is a sink; from inside, it is a source. One filter decides every drop, and at a boundary it gets all four answers wrong — it refuses both legal wirings and accepts both illegal ones. The second bug is unrelated and smaller: a state SystemSketch invented, which neither starter kit has, has exits that nobody enumerated. Both are reproduced below in the real app, and both are already solved in code you own.

6 / 8 checks reproduced the report headless Chrome · real pointer events tldraw 5.3.2 fix already exists in pyblocks feature already exists in the kit

So bug 2 is session-lifetime corruption, not file corruption.

2 · Root cause — one filter, four wrong answers

In SystemSketch a port's side is its terminal. That equation is the whole bug: it is true for a leaf Block and false for a boundary.

// connectionModel.ts — a port's side IS its terminal. One port, one direction.
export function terminalForBlockPortSide(side: 'input' | 'output'): ConnectionTerminal {
  return side === 'output' ? 'start' : 'end'
}
// ConnectionShapeUtil.tsx — onHandleDrag, the only place a drop finds a port.
const terminal = handle.id as ConnectionTerminal            // the FREE end
const target = getBlockConnectionPortAtPoint(this.editor, pagePoint, { terminal })

// blockPorts.ts — and the filter that decides.
for (const port of getBlockConnectionPorts(shape.props)) {
  if (options.terminal !== undefined && port.terminal !== options.terminal) continue
  ...
}
press  run.in_1              side 'input'   → terminal 'end'
       origin.terminal = 'end'
       draggingTerminal = opposite('end') = 'start'          ← the free handle

drop   getBlockConnectionPortAtPoint(p, { terminal: 'start' })
       decode.in_1          side 'input'   → terminal 'end'  ← 'end' !== 'start'
       CONTINUE  ── the only candidate under the pointer is skipped

       target === null
       → removeConnectionBinding(...)  and the free end just follows the mouse
Your hypothesis was right, and understated. It is not that input→input is blocked; it is that at a boundary the polarity is inverted. The filter refuses the two wirings a hierarchy needs and accepts the two it must not — and nothing in the model can express the difference, because a port's side is its terminal.

The fix you already wrote

pyblocks solved this months ago, in the words you used in the FR: a boundary port grows an inner face — a derived twin at the same anchor with the flipped terminal, live only in the Expanded view. Exactly one of the two faces matches any given drag, so there is no ambiguity to resolve and no new dot on screen.

// pyblocks · nodes/types/blockModel.ts — the whole fix, 12 lines.
export const INNER_PORT_SUFFIX = '__inner'

/**
 * Derive the inner-face twin of every anchored port — flipped terminal, same
 * anchor. Twins exist in EVERY view (a cable welded to one must survive view
 * switches) but are hidden outside `expanded`, where the inside is wired.
 */
function addInnerFacePorts(ports: Record<string, ShapePort>, view: BlockView) {
  for (const id of Object.keys(ports)) {
    if (isInnerPortId(id)) continue
    const outer = ports[id]
    const hidden = view !== 'expanded' || outer.hidden === true
    ports[innerPortId(id)] = {
      id: innerPortId(id),
      x: outer.x, y: outer.y,                                   // SAME anchor
      terminal: outer.terminal === 'start' ? 'end' : 'start',   // FLIPPED
      dataType: outer.dataType,
      inner: true,
      ...(hidden ? { hidden: true } : null),
    }
  }
}

// pyblocks · ports/Port.tsx — and which face a press starts from.
onPointerDown={() => {
  // In the expanded view the dot's press wires the INSIDE (the inner face is
  // what an internal drag can land on both ends of); outer cables are made
  // from the other block's dot, exactly as before.
  const active = innerFace ?? port
  editor.setCurrentTool('select.pointing_port', {
    shapeId, portId: active.id, terminal: active.terminal, dataType: active.dataType,
  })
}}

3 · Root cause — a state with an unenumerated exit

Bug 2 has nothing to do with ports. SystemSketch invented a gesture neither starter kit has: a tap on a port arms a cable that follows the pointer with no button held. Four ways out of that state clean up after themselves. Two do not — and they are the two you reach by changing tool.

// PointingBlockPort.ts — SystemSketch's own invention: a tap arms a cable that
// follows the pointer with no button held, until the next press.
override onPointerUp(info: TLPointerEventInfo): void {
  const created = origin ? createConnectionFromPort(this.editor, this.info, origin) : null
  this.parent.transition('connecting_block_port', created)      // ← armed
}

export class ConnectingBlockPort extends StateNode {
  onCancel(info)    { this.abandon(info) }   // Escape        → bailToMark ✓
  onComplete(info)  { this.abandon(info) }   // Enter         → bailToMark ✓
  onInterrupt(info) { if (!this.committed) this.abandon(info) }
  onPointerDown(info) { ...bailToMark if not both terminals... }  //           ✓

  onExit(): void {
    this.editor.setCursor({ type: 'default', rotation: 0 })      // ← and that is all
  }
}
// tldraw 5.3.2 · Editor.ts — a tool shortcut is a plain root transition.
setCurrentTool(id: string, info = {}): this {
  this.root.transition(id, info)     // runs onExit on the whole active branch.
  return this                        // dispatches NO cancel / complete / interrupt.
}
Leaving the armed state by…RouteResult
Escapecancel event → onCancelbails the mark
Entercomplete event → onCompletebails the mark
click on empty canvaspointer-down → onPointerDownbails the mark
press A (or any tool key)root.transition('arrow') → onExitorphan cable survives
click another toolbar toolroot.transition(…) → onExitorphan cable survives
switch page / undo / delete the Blockno event reaches the stateunproven, same shape
Why enumerating exits is the wrong fix. Adding a bail to onExit closes the two rows above and leaves the class open — onExit also runs on transitions where bailing would be wrong, and a state that outlives its gesture will keep growing exits as the app grows. The kit's answer is to not have the state.

4 · The same edit is the feature you asked for

In the kits, a tap on a port and a drag that lands on nothing both open the on-canvas picker — the behaviour in your third screenshot. Deleting the armed state is what frees the click gesture to do it.

// image-pipeline kit · ports/PointingPort.tsx — there is no armed state at all.
export class PointingPort extends StateNode {
  static override id = 'pointing_port'

  onPointerMove(info) { if (dragging) this.parent.transition('dragging_handle', {...}) }
  onPointerUp(info)   { this.onClick(); this.parent.transition('idle', info) }
  //                    └── opens the on-canvas node picker anchored to the cable
}

// ConnectionShapeUtil.tsx — and a drag that lands on nothing does the same.
onHandleDragEnd(connection, { handle, isCreatingShape }) {
  if (bindings[draggingTerminal]) return
  if (isCreatingShape && draggingTerminal === 'end') {
    onCanvasNodePickerState.set(this.editor, {
      connectionShapeId: connection.id,
      location: draggingTerminal,
      onClose: () => { if (!bindings.start || !bindings.end) this.editor.deleteShapes([...]) },
      onPick: (nodeType, terminalInPageSpace) => { /* create + auto-bind first compatible port */ },
    })
  } else {
    if (!bindings.start || !bindings.end) this.editor.deleteShapes([connection.id])
  }
}

5 · Where the code should come from

A finding worth stating plainly: pyblocks src/pipeline/ is the image-pipeline starter kit — its own fileBackedBoard.tsx says so — carrying several weeks of fixes on top. So “start from the kits” and “take the learnings from pyblocks” are not two sources to reconcile; they are the same lineage, and the second is strictly ahead of the first. Today's SystemSketch cable is a hand-trimmed re-derivation that dropped almost all of it. That trim is why the bugs are re-appearing one at a time.

One measurement worth keeping: a caller's margin is ignored on tldraw's open-geometry branch — getShapeAtPoint hits when distanceToPoint(p) < hitTestMargin / zoom and nothing else. Widening a cable's clickable corridor therefore cannot be done from a call site; it has to be done by padding the geometry. That is what the HitPadded* mixin exists for.

6 · The plan

Six phases, each one shippable and each one provable in the real app. Phases 0–2 are the ones that answer this report; 3–5 are the FR's own § Edges. Everything happens in ?preset=block-dev and promotes to Stable at the end of phase 2 and phase 5.

0

Land the donor, unchanged

half a day

Every later phase is cheap only if the shared vocabulary is the kit's. Port the kit's ports/ + connection/ module boundary into src/blocks/connections/ as-is, then re-point it at the SystemSketch block shape instead of the kit's node.

  • ports/portState.ts, ports/getPortAtPoint.ts, ports/Port.tsx, connection/* arrive with their kit names, so a future diff against a re-scaffolded kit still works.
  • getBlockConnectionPorts() becomes the getNodePorts() equivalent: a createComputedCache keyed on the Block record.
  • getNodePortConnections() arrives with it — the cached table the port dot, the inspector and (later) the Python analyzer all read.

Proof The four existing connection unit suites still pass, plus the current real-browser journeys. No behaviour change is claimed.

1

Boundary inner faces — the reported bug

half a day

Your own words: “when you are inside the box, the input port becomes like an output port once you are inside the boundary.” That is exactly what pyblocks already ships, and it is 12 lines.

  • addInnerFacePorts() derives a …__inner twin per port: same anchor, flipped terminal, hidden outside the Expanded view.
  • The port dot draws once and carries the union of both faces' connected / hinting / eligible state, so nothing new appears on screen.
  • A press on a boundary dot in Expanded view starts from the inner face; a press from outside still starts from the outer one.
  • reparentConnectionToBoundary() gains the both-ends-on-one-block case, so a straight-through in_1__inner → out_1__inner wire parents inside the block.

Proof tests/boundary_port_edge_diagnosis.mjs flips from 4 REPRO to 4 ok on the truth table — it already asserts the desired column.

2

Delete the armed state; adopt the picker

one day

The bug and the feature you asked for are the same edit. The kit has no armed tap-to-place state — a tap opens the node picker, and a drag that lands on nothing opens the same picker at the loose end.

  • ConnectingBlockPort is deleted. With it goes every un-enumerable exit path, because there is no longer a state that outlives the gesture.
  • PointingBlockPort keeps exactly two exits: dragging_handle on a drag, idle on a tap.
  • onHandleDragEnd with no binding on the dragged terminal opens OnCanvasBlockPicker anchored to that terminal; onClose deletes a still-half-bound cable.
  • onPick creates the Block, offsets it so its first compatible port lands under the cable end, and binds — the image-pipeline behaviour in your screenshot.
  • The picker lists SystemSketch Block presets, not the kit's node zoo. Inside an Expanded block it stands down on an inner face (pyblocks already does this: the picker would place the new Block outside the boundary).

Proof New browser journey: drag to empty canvas → picker → pick → a bound cable and a placed Block. Plus BUG-2a/2b flip to ok, and a fuzz pass that leaves the gesture by every exit in the table and asserts zero half-bound cables.

3

Refusal, and showing it

one day

Today the only feedback for an illegal drop is that nothing happens — which is indistinguishable from a missed target. The kit answers this with two port states and a veto list.

  • portState arrives: eligiblePorts lights every port a drag could legally land on the moment it starts; hintingPort lights the one under the pointer.
  • Vetoes: wrong terminal, cycle, and (once Block ports carry a type) type mismatch. Hierarchy edges are exempt from the cycle veto — a child feeding its parent's inner face is the hierarchy working, not a loop.
  • An occupied single-connection input is replaced at drop, not doubled; the replacement is deferred to onHandleDragEnd so an abandoned drag never destroys the wire it hovered.

Proof Journey asserts the eligible set is painted, an illegal drop leaves no cable, and a legal drop onto an occupied input leaves exactly one.

4

The hit profile you already chose

half a day

You picked these numbers on 2026-08-27 against a live A/B gallery. They are the answer to “the clickable region is really thin”, and they are the “port target zones” you asked me to bring over.

  • connectionHit.ts ports across whole: the three profiles, the padded geometry mixin, and the constants derived from the port dot's own CSS.
  • Default profile pyblocks: cable corridor ±9u, port snap 18u, per-port model, reconnect 10u.
  • Wired-port precedence: pressing within 10u of a port that already has a cable moves that cable rather than starting a new one.

Proof The existing pure unit tests come with the file. The browser journey re-measures the port dot's outer radius out of the running app rather than trusting the constant.

5

The edge editor

two days

This is the FR's own § Edges: three routings, control points, Figma's show-on-select-and-near rule, labels, error state.

  • Elbow routing with the A* + authored-route persistence from pyblocks, including the fix that keeps a segment perpendicular to the block side it leaves.
  • Splice / rail handles; the centre + that inserts a Block into a cable (ConnectionCenterHandleOverlayUtil + insertNodeWithinConnection, both straight from the kit).
  • keepConnectionsAtBottom so cables paint under Blocks, per parent — which is what makes an Expanded block's internal wiring readable.
  • Routing becomes a StyleProp (it already is) so the inspector and a multi-selection batch it for free.

Proof Golden geometry tests per routing kind, plus a journey per control-point gesture.

Do Block ports get a data type?The Block model has port.type as a free string today (Frame, raw bytes). The kit's compatibility veto needs a closed enum. I would keep the free string and skip the type veto until the Python backend defines the type lattice — an editor that refuses a cable on a guess is worse than one that accepts it. Phase 3 ships the cycle veto and the terminal veto only.my call — say the word and I'll wire types instead
Should a boundary port draw two dots or one?pyblocks draws one: the dot is the port, and the inner face is a second identity at the same anchor. That keeps the Expanded frame edge clean and matches your “only the circle of the port should be visible outside the frame” note. The cost is that you cannot see, at a glance, whether the inside or the outside is wired.my call — one dot, union state
Straight-through wires (in_1__inner → out_1__inner)Both ends on the same Block. pyblocks allows it and parents the cable inside that Block. It is how you draw a pass-through, so I would keep it.my call — allowed

8 · What the harness actually drove

Every line below is a real gesture in the real product build, read back from the painted document. No editor API was called to make a cable, and no component was rendered in isolation.

  1. the reported scene is built through real gestures: an Expanded run with a boundary port, a nested decode with its ownBlock tool, real drag, real inspector clicks — nested confirmed from the painted DOM.
  2. run.in → decode.in — the exact gesture from your screenshot — creates no cable0 cables. The reported bug, reproduced.
  3. decode.out → run.out also creates no cableThe same root cause on the other half of the boundary; not in your report, and just as broken.
  4. decode.out → run.in does create a cableData leaving the box through its own inlet. The polarity is not strict — it is inverted.
  5. run.out → decode.in does create a cableAn outlet acting as a source for the inside.
  6. a tap on a port arms a cable that follows the pointer with no button heldselect.connecting_block_port, a SystemSketch invention neither kit has.
  7. pressing A leaves the half-bound cable in the documentBug 2, reproduced — and the arrow tool is now active over an orphaned cable.
  8. clicking a different toolbar tool leaves it tooSo the leak is the transition, not the keyboard.
  9. Escape does clean up — the controlThe state's own bail path works; it is simply never reached by a tool change.
  10. the orphan does not survive a reloadcleanupStaleConnections prunes half-bound cables at install. Session-lifetime corruption, not file corruption.
